No options or RSUs are included. A shareholder proposal printed in the proxy says he owns '14% of the economic value'; that is the proponent's statement, not the company's, and is not used. 5% HOLDERS: the proxy states their percentages as % of Class A only (Vanguard 8.5%, BlackRock 7.2%, FMR 6.1%), and those are the figures recorded in pctEconomic. studies.title: Meta's Economic Contribution in the U.S. (2024)

ecosystem.notes: The 10-K has no flow measure, so measure is null. The study is Meta's own ("a new study we conducted", announced May 13, 2025) and covers the U.S. only. It starts from Meta's estimate that each U.S. ad dollar yields $3.71 of advertiser revenue ("over $215 billion in business/advertisers revenues in the U.S. from Meta ads"), then applies BEA input-output multipliers for indirect and induced activity, so the $548 billion is a modelled economic-activity figure, not money paid to businesses or creators. It includes about $2 billion of Meta's own non-advertising sales. A separate Meta study puts the EU figure at €213 billion and 1.44 million jobs in 2024; it is not added here. Meta revenue is worldwide, so it is not comparable with the U.S.-only study figure.

footprint.notes: usStates: one row per state from Meta's own 'Meta in <State>' fact sheets (research.facebook.com/economiccontribution, 50 states; no DC sheet), each read in full. Output and jobs are Meta's modelled estimates of activity at advertisers and their supply chains linked to Meta ads (BEA input-output multipliers), not Meta payroll or spending; the national sheet gives $547.6 billion and 3,400,000 jobs. research.facebook.com refuses scripted requests, so the 50 PDFs were opened in a real browser (each redirects to a signed fbcdn.net copy, downloaded and read); source.url is the stable research.facebook.com/file/... address, which the automated quote checker cannot fetch. Sites: corporate HQ from the 10-K (which says Meta owns 27 data center locations), plus data centers from datacenters.atmeta.com (page read Nov 2026, undated, and it lists sites announced after FY2024). Selection rule: every data center outside North America, and the seven U.S. data centers with the largest stated investment, limited to sites that broke ground in 2024 or earlier; newer announced sites (Lebanon IN, El Paso TX, Bowling Green OH, Beaver Dam WI, Tulsa OK, Sturgeon County AB) are left out. Several states host more than one data center (AL, IN, OH, TX), so data-center figures are not summed into states. Long-lived assets: the 10-K discloses only the U.S. and the rest of the world. Revenue by geography is in the records and not repeated.
